To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

trustees respond to (un)reasonable requests in a self-bounded way, but not in a self-interested way, and that they do not systematically respond to increasing requests in a way that would make them more trustworthy.
“Trustors are more willing to trust if the trustee’s request is static or dynamic reasonable, and if the trustee is not too greedy”.
(1) static reasonableness of the requests matters in a selfbiased way, and (2) dynamic reasonableness matters too, in the sense of a decreasing trend.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how trustors respond to requests that are reasonable or unreasonable in a static sense, and how they respond to a sequence of reasonable or unreasonable requests.
the question of whether it is better to be a trustee in a world where requests are static and reasonable, or in a world where they are dynamic and reasonable.
the interplay of trust and norms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the more reasonable the requests are, the less trustworthy the trustees become.
the more reasonable the request, the more the trustee is willing to return, but the less he is willing to trust.
the more a request seems reasonable, the more it is returned, but this statement is only partially true, since it does not apply to the case of increasing requests.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more a trustee is asked for, the more he/she will give. But the more a trustee gives, the less he/she will
the norm of reasonable behavior matters for trustworthiness, and that the norm can be defined in terms of static and dynamic properties.
the norm of what is reasonable to return to a trustor is not a static concept, but a dynamic one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when designing a trust game experiment, one should be aware that the sequence of requests matters.
the norm of what is considered to be a reasonable request matters, and that this norm is not necessarily aligned with what is expected from trustors.
trustworthiness depends not only on the level of each request, but also on the sequence of requests.
